paragraphs: The paper examines whether compact descriptions of a decision problem also permit compact descriptions of its solutions. Its setting is factored Markov decision processes, where the dynamics have a structured representation. The central distinction is between the difficulty of computing a policy and the difficulty of representing that policy once it has been found.

The authors establish a hardness result using a fixed family of factored problems with linear rewards. For this family, optimal policies and value functions cannot be represented succinctly in standard parametric forms. Thus, a compact account of how the system changes and assigns rewards does not guarantee an equally compact account of how to act or what outcomes are worth.

Earlier computational hardness results left open the possibility that compact solutions existed but were difficult to discover. This result addresses that possibility directly. It also extends to policies providing even a polynomially poor approximation to optimal value and identifies connections to Arthur–Merlin complexity. The implication concerns the constructed family: choosing a function approximator can encounter a representational obstacle before optimization even begins.
neurips-2002-a-note-on-the-representatio.tldr: A hardness result shows that some compactly described factored decision problems lack compact policy and value representations, even for weak approximations.

paragraphs: Recognizing spontaneous facial behavior requires handling more than deliberately posed expressions. People turn and nod their heads, changing how facial movements appear to a camera. This project explores how to recognize those movements when the face rotates out of the image plane, moving beyond collection conditions that require subjects to face the camera.

The proposed front end uses three-dimensional tracking and image warping to transform facial images into standardized views. Support vector machines and hidden Markov models then operate on the warped images. This arrangement makes viewpoint handling part of the recognition process, so the learning methods can work with images brought into a more consistent orientation.

The prototype was tested on a set of movements defined by the Facial Action Coding System. The authors describe the combined tracking, warping, and learning approach as viable and promising for spontaneous expression recognition. They also report that filters derived from image statistics captured information about movement dynamics. These findings support the approach as ongoing prototype work, rather than establishing complete recognition of spontaneous facial behavior.
neurips-2002-a-prototype-for-automatic-r.tldr: A prototype combines 3D face tracking and image warping with learned classifiers to recognize spontaneous facial actions despite head rotation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to calculate bootstrap averages used to estimate generalization error: how well a learned predictor performs beyond its training observations. The quantity of interest is an average over bootstrap resampling. The authors investigate an analytical approximation to that average, bringing methods from statistical physics into the assessment of predictive models.

Their approach combines the replica method with a variational method. Together, these tools provide a way to approximate the desired average through mathematical analysis. The contribution is therefore a method for evaluating bootstrap quantities, with generalization-error estimation as its purpose, rather than a new predictor trained directly for the regression task.

The authors demonstrate the approach using Gaussian process regression and compare its results with averages obtained through Monte Carlo sampling. This comparison connects the analytical calculation to a sampling-based calculation of the target quantities. The stated contribution is an approximate analytical route and its demonstration in that setting; the abstract reports the comparison without claiming a particular accuracy advantage, speedup, or exact agreement.
neurips-2002-a-statistical-mechanics-app.tldr: The paper combines replica and variational methods to approximate bootstrap averages for generalization-error estimation in Gaussian process regression.

paragraphs: This paper treats classification as an inference problem that may need to adapt as observations arrive. Instead of viewing a classifier's parameters as permanently fixed, it models them as hidden states in a first-order Markov process. The current parameter state is therefore linked to the preceding state, providing a probabilistic description of how the classifier evolves.

The resulting algorithm is a variational extension of Kalman filtering for generalized nonlinear classification. It aims to combine the computational benefits of a parametric representation with flexibility associated with sequential sampling. Two new lower bounds make it possible to retain a non-degenerate distribution over the adaptation rate, representing uncertainty about adaptation instead of collapsing it to one fixed value.

The empirical evaluation reports competitive classifiers in both stationary environments and environments that change over time. This supports the method's use across those two settings without implying that adaptation always improves performance. Although classification is the focus, the authors also state that the algorithm extends easily to other generalized nonlinear models, making the inference construction broader than the particular task studied.
neurips-2002-adaptive-classification-by-.tldr: A variational Kalman filter adapts nonlinear classifiers by treating their parameters and adaptation rate probabilistically.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a mixture model for analog data whose probabilistic meaning and learning behavior come from the operation of transistors. Called the bump mixture model, it connects statistical modeling directly to a silicon implementation. The hardware's behavior helps define the model itself, linking the mathematical description to the physical mechanism that performs inference and adaptation.

Translinear circuits carry out probabilistic inference, while floating-gate devices provide adaptation. The system is described as low power, asynchronous, and fully parallel, and it supports several learning algorithms on the chip. The same mixture-model framework can be used for probability estimation, vector quantization, classification, and clustering, giving the circuit a range of statistical roles.

The authors tested fabricated hardware on clustering, quantization, and handwritten-digit classification. They report performance comparable to expectation-maximization applied to Gaussian mixtures. The result shows that a statistical system derived from transistor behavior can carry out these learning tasks with competitive performance in the reported tests. Its significance lies in combining an implemented adaptive circuit with a coherent probabilistic model.
neurips-2002-adaptive-quantization-and-d.tldr: A transistor-derived mixture model performs probabilistic learning in silicon, with reported performance comparable to Gaussian-mixture EM on tested tasks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how a kernelized support vector machine can determine which input variables matter. It represents each variable's relevance through a scale factor that helps define the geometry of the input space. Changing these factors changes how input differences are measured, making feature relevance part of the classifier's own representation.

The algorithm learns the scale factors alongside the usual classifier parameters by minimizing the standard SVM empirical risk. Constraints encourage a sparse set of scales, with irrelevant variables receiving zero weight. A variable with zero scale no longer contributes to the input metric, so feature selection arises directly from the same procedure that tunes the classifier.

The authors report favorable comparisons with leading feature-selection procedures and demonstrate the method on a demanding facial-expression recognition task. These results support the usefulness of adapting the input metric while learning the decision rule. The key contribution is the integration: identifying relevant variables and fitting a kernel classifier become coupled parts of one optimization approach.
neurips-2002-adaptive-scaling-for-featur.tldr: The method selects SVM input features by learning sparse scale factors that adapt the input-space metric during classifier training.

paragraphs: The paper develops a model of short-term synaptic depression from an implemented silicon circuit. Depression describes a temporary reduction in a synapse's response during activity. Deriving the model from hardware connects its mathematical description to the behavior of a physical system, allowing the equations and circuit measurements to be examined together.

The circuit's dynamics resemble those of some existing theoretical depression models, but its recovery behaves differently. Recovery is nonlinear and depends on the frequency of presynaptic activity. These features make the rate of incoming activity relevant to the evolution of depression, rather than treating recovery as a process independent of that frequency.

The equations fit both steady-state and transient measurements from a fabricated network containing leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and different synapse types. The authors also present experimental data about possible computational roles of depression. One proposed role is that input through a depressing synapse can rapidly bring a neuron toward its firing threshold when its membrane potential starts near rest. This is presented as a possible function, alongside the model's agreement with circuit behavior.
neurips-2002-circuit-model-of-short-term.tldr: A silicon-derived synaptic depression model fits circuit measurements and suggests how depressing synapses may help rapidly bring resting neurons to threshold.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Coulomb classifiers through an analogy with charged conductors in electrostatics. Each training example corresponds to a conductor at a particular location, the classification function corresponds to electric potential, and the training objective corresponds to Coulomb energy. This creates a common framework that includes two established support-vector-machine formulations.

The analogy serves both to explain relationships among existing methods and to suggest new ones. The authors describe kernels connecting polynomial and radial-basis functions, objectives that do not require positive-definite kernels, and regularization that permits construction of an optimal classifier in Minkowski space. These possibilities arise from reconsidering classifier design through the physical framework.

The paper develops new SVMs from these ideas and evaluates them in simulations. Reported performance is comparable to or better than standard SVMs in the tested settings. The experiments include classification from pairwise proximity representations, where a Coulomb classifier outperformed standard SVMs. The findings support the framework as a source of useful algorithms as well as an interpretation of familiar ones.
neurips-2002-coulomb-classifiers-general.tldr: An electrostatic interpretation unifies established SVMs and motivates new classifiers with competitive or better performance in the reported simulations.

paragraphs: The paper tests a previously proposed neurotrophic model of how two forms of visual organization develop together. Topography concerns the spatial organization of visual inputs, while ocular dominance columns concern organization by eye preference in primary visual cortex. The question is whether the model can develop both structures when driven by signals from physical neuronal vision sensors.

The experiment uses a pair of sensors stimulated with disparate moving patterns. Their outputs are spike trains, and the timing relationships between those spikes provide the input to the plasticity model. This links the developmental model to temporally structured sensory activity produced by the devices, including imperfections in those signals.

The authors report that temporal correlations between the two sensors' spike trains elicit refined topography and ocular dominance columns. These structures develop even with substantial spontaneous activity and fixed-pattern sensor noise. The result supports the model's ability to produce the two kinds of organization under the tested noisy input conditions and highlights correlated spike timing as the relevant signal in this demonstration.
neurips-2002-developing-topography-and-o.tldr: Correlated spikes from two noisy silicon vision sensors drive a plasticity model to develop refined visual topography and ocular dominance columns.

paragraphs: The paper studies how boosting can learn to assign labels to sequences. The learning objective uses a sequence rank loss, making the ranking of candidate label sequences central to training. This focuses the method on structured predictions in which the output is an entire sequence of labels, rather than a single category.

The proposed algorithm combines boosting with the computational efficiency of dynamic programming. The authors also discuss alternatives based on Hamming loss, which assesses disagreement at individual sequence positions. Considering these losses makes the treatment of prediction errors an explicit part of the method: ranking whole label sequences and counting positionwise errors provide different training perspectives.

Experiments on named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging demonstrate the approach's validity and competitiveness. The paper presents sequence boosting as an alternative to methods based on hidden Markov models and conditional random fields. It also identifies information extraction, natural language processing, and computational biology as application areas. The stated empirical findings support the method on the two reported language tasks without claiming universal superiority across sequence problems.
neurips-2002-discriminative-learning-for.tldr: Sequence boosting combines a ranking-based learning objective with dynamic programming and shows competitive results on two language-labeling tasks.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to obtain provably exact maximum a posteriori estimates for a subclass of graphical problems containing cycles. A MAP estimate is the configuration with the greatest probability. The approach expresses the original cyclic problem as a convex combination of tree-structured problems, connecting its optimum to optima of the component problems.

Convexity provides an upper bound on the original optimal log probability using the combined tree optima. The authors prove that this bound is reached exactly if and only if all component problems share an optimal configuration. Whenever such agreement exists, the shared configuration is also optimal for the original graph. Agreement therefore provides a certificate of exactness.

The authors develop a tree-reweighted max-product algorithm that attempts to find a decomposition with this shared optimum. They also give necessary and sufficient conditions for an algorithmic fixed point to yield the exact MAP estimate. The analysis extends naturally to combinations of hypertree-structured distributions. The exactness guarantee depends on the stated agreement conditions; the search procedure is not asserted to solve every cyclic problem.
neurips-2002-exact-map-estimates-by-hype.tldr: Agreement among optimal configurations of tree-structured subproblems certifies an exact MAP solution for the original cyclic graph.

paragraphs: Selecting useful attributes for clustering is difficult because there are no class labels to indicate which distinctions matter. This paper addresses that problem within Gaussian mixture clustering. It proposes two ways to assess feature relevance while learning groups from the data, making the choice of attributes part of the unsupervised modeling process.

The first approach estimates feature saliencies rather than immediately making binary include-or-exclude decisions. The authors derive an expectation-maximization algorithm for this estimation. This gives the model a way to express degrees of relevance, allowing the treatment of features to be learned alongside the mixture-based account of the data.

The second approach extends a mutual-information relevance criterion to the unsupervised setting and uses backward search to select features. It is a wrapper method: an outer feature-selection procedure surrounds mixture estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real data show promising performance for both approaches. Together, the methods offer two distinct routes to the same objective—estimating relevance within the model or searching over feature choices around it.
neurips-2002-feature-selection-in-mixtur.tldr: Two methods select useful clustering features through EM-based saliency estimation or a mutual-information wrapper around Gaussian mixture fitting.

paragraphs: The paper starts from a distinction between AdaBoost's training objective and the practical aim of classification. AdaBoost minimizes an exponential upper bound related to training margins, while applications ultimately care about classification error. Learning effective weak classifiers is another challenge, especially when the input has many dimensions.

FloatBoost adds a backtracking step after each AdaBoost iteration. This step removes weak classifiers that cause higher error rates, allowing earlier ensemble choices to be reconsidered as training proceeds. The authors also propose a statistical method for learning weak classifiers through a stagewise approximation to posterior probabilities using an overcomplete collection of scalar features.

The experimental application is face detection, where the classifier must distinguish face from nonface patterns in a high-dimensional space. In the reported comparisons, FloatBoost uses fewer weak classifiers while achieving lower training and test error than AdaBoost. These findings support revisiting ensemble membership as a way to improve both compactness and accuracy in the tested task. They establish an empirical benefit, rather than a guarantee for every boosting problem.
neurips-2002-floatboost-learning-for-cla.tldr: FloatBoost revisits and removes weak classifiers during boosting, producing smaller ensembles with lower reported training and test error on face detection.

paragraphs: The paper considers forecasting several steps ahead in a nonlinear time series using a Gaussian process model. One way to make such a forecast is to repeatedly apply a one-step predictor. As this process continues, earlier predicted outputs become inputs to later predictions, linking the steps of the forecast.

Using only point estimates for those intermediate outputs leaves their uncertainty out of the later input representation. The paper develops an analytical Gaussian approximation that incorporates uncertainty about these intermediate regressor values. In this setting, regressors are the quantities supplied to the predictor, including previous outputs that must themselves be estimated.

The method updates uncertainty on the current prediction while accounting for uncertain inputs inherited from preceding steps. Its central contribution is a formal treatment of uncertainty within repeated forecasting, connecting uncertainty about what enters the model to uncertainty about what it predicts. The construction remains an approximation, as stated by the authors, and the abstract presents it as a methodological contribution rather than reporting a numerical forecasting improvement.
neurips-2002-gaussian-process-priors-wit.tldr: An analytical Gaussian approximation propagates uncertainty in intermediate inputs through repeated Gaussian process time-series forecasts.

paragraphs: This study aims to improve the information transfer rate of an EEG-based brain–computer interface. It builds on an existing approach and analyzes recorded data offline, using a setup intended to be closer to online operation than the original studies. The practical objective is to extract usable information from the signals more efficiently.

The authors pursue two improvements. First, they use support vector machines for signal classification and combine several classifications by accumulating the values of the classification function. This combines the classifier's outputs across decisions. Second, they increase the number of electrodes, expanding the signal information available to the learning system.

Accumulating classifier values produced significantly improved transfer rates relative to the techniques used in the original work. Together with the added electrodes, the approach achieved an average of 50.5 bits per minute and a maximum of 84.7 bits per minute. These are results from the stated offline analysis, even though the setup was designed to more closely resemble online use. The study shows benefits from improving both signal interpretation and the available measurements.
neurips-2002-improving-transfer-rates-in.tldr: Offline EEG analysis combining accumulated SVM outputs with more electrodes achieved average and maximum transfer rates of 50.5 and 84.7 bits per minute.

paragraphs: The paper applies probabilistic learning to automatically identify classes of galaxies using their shapes and pixel intensities. A key part of the problem is spatial orientation: the method learns how to align a collection of galaxies geometrically. This makes alignment an inferred component of the analysis rather than requiring the images to arrive already oriented consistently.

Expectation-maximization is used to learn this alignment through an ordering model. The authors augment that model with a mixture model over objects, allowing different galaxy classes to be represented. A two-level EM procedure then learns the classes without supervision, bringing geometric alignment and the discovery of groups into a combined probabilistic framework.

The resulting models provide highly accurate galaxy classification in the reported cross-validation experiments. The finding supports the usefulness of combining orientation learning with class learning for this image task. Both shape and intensity contribute to the model, while the alignment mechanism gives those characteristics a consistent geometric context. The empirical claim concerns the evaluated models and experiments, with no numerical accuracy specified in the abstract.
neurips-2002-learning-to-classify-galaxy.tldr: A two-level EM model jointly learns galaxy alignment and unsupervised classes, yielding highly accurate classification in reported cross-validation experiments.

paragraphs: The paper asks how two approaches to clustering are related. The information bottleneck constructs a representation that retains information about another variable. Maximum likelihood fits a probabilistic mixture model to data. Although their starting points differ, both produce structure by grouping observations, motivating a mathematical comparison of their objectives.

The authors define a mapping between the information bottleneck problem and maximum likelihood for a multinomial mixture model. Under this mapping, they establish a strong relationship. For a uniform input distribution or a large sample size, the problems are mathematically equivalent. These are the conditions attached to the equivalence, rather than a claim that arbitrary clustering formulations coincide.

More specifically, every fixed point of one objective corresponds to a fixed point of the other in these cases. Objective values at those points also match after simple transformations. Consequently, an algorithm solving either problem induces a solution to the other under the stated conditions. The result gives a precise bridge between an information-theoretic clustering principle and a statistical mixture-model formulation.
neurips-2002-maximum-likelihood-and-the-.tldr: A mapping establishes conditional equivalence between information bottleneck clustering and maximum likelihood for multinomial mixture models.

paragraphs: The paper develops a robust controller-design method for systems with high-dimensional state spaces. It combines differential dynamic programming with a minimax criterion, bringing robustness to disturbances into policy design. The approach is demonstrated on a simulated five-link biped robot, where the policy must generate joint control actions that sustain walking.

The reported optimal policy uses lower joint torques than a hand-tuned proportional–derivative servo controller. The simulated robot also continues walking under unknown disturbances that cause both standard differential dynamic programming controllers and the hand-tuned servo to fail. These comparisons address two practical aspects of the resulting behavior: the required joint torques and the ability to withstand disturbances.

The authors further demonstrate learning to compensate for modeling errors and previously unknown disturbances in conjunction with robust control design. This combines a policy designed for robustness with adjustment based on discrepancies encountered by the system. The findings show benefits in the simulated walking example, supporting the proposed design method without extending the demonstrated result to every disturbance or to a physical robot.
neurips-2002-minimax-differential-dynami.tldr: Minimax differential dynamic programming produces a simulated biped controller that withstands tested unknown disturbances and uses lower torques than a hand-tuned servo.

paragraphs: The paper predicts protein structure through contact or distance maps, which describe relationships between parts of a protein. These representations stay the same when the protein is translated or rotated. A contact map records neighborhood relationships, while a distance map records pairwise distances, allowing the prediction target to express structure without depending on spatial orientation.

The methods use generalized input-output hidden Markov models and generalized recursive neural networks. For fine-grained representations, topology is predicted directly at the amino-acid or atomic scale. For coarse representations built from secondary-structure elements, the method first learns to score candidate graphs, then uses that scoring function to search possible configurations.

Computer simulations report state-of-the-art predictive performance. The two prediction routes adapt the learning strategy to the chosen structural resolution: direct map prediction for fine detail and learned scoring with search for coarser arrangements. The contribution concerns predicting topological representations that capture structural relationships. Its use of invariant targets addresses the fact that a protein's structure should not depend on where it is placed or how it is turned.
neurips-2002-prediction-of-protein-topol.tldr: Generalized hidden Markov models and recursive neural networks predict invariant protein contact or distance maps, with reported state-of-the-art simulation results.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the separation of a single image into shading and reflectance components. Shading describes appearance changes associated with illumination, while reflectance concerns changes in the surface itself. The algorithm approaches this separation by deciding which of these two causes accounts for local changes in the observed image.

It combines color information with a classifier trained to recognize grayscale patterns. These cues are used to classify each image derivative as arising from shading or a reflectance change. Working with derivatives focuses the decision on changes across the image, providing local evidence for how the two underlying components should be separated.

Some locations offer clearer evidence than others. Generalized belief propagation carries information from confident areas into ambiguous ones, allowing the decomposition to use relationships beyond each isolated local decision. The authors show results on real images. The contribution is a combination of complementary visual cues and information propagation for recovering intrinsic images from one observation, with the reported demonstrations establishing application to real imagery.
neurips-2002-recovering-intrinsic-images.tldr: The algorithm combines color, learned grayscale cues, and generalized belief propagation to separate shading from reflectance in a single image.

paragraphs: Agents with aligned interests can still struggle to coordinate when a game has several Nash equilibria. Reaching an equilibrium does not by itself mean selecting an optimal coordinated policy. The challenge becomes greater when agents initially do not know the game and each receives noisy payoff observations, making both learning the environment and learning how to act necessary.

The paper introduces optimal adaptive learning to address these connected problems in team Markov games. Its central result is convergence to an optimal Nash equilibrium with probability one in any game within that class, under the convergence conditions. This is a claim about eventual learning behavior, with optimality of the equilibrium included in the guarantee.

The authors supply a convergence proof and state that the algorithm's parameters are easy to set to satisfy the required conditions. The contribution therefore combines an algorithm with a theoretical account of successful coordination. It shows how the uncertainty involved in identifying the game can be handled alongside the task of learning to play an optimal equilibrium.
neurips-2002-reinforcement-learning-to-p.tldr: Optimal adaptive learning provably converges with probability one to an optimal Nash equilibrium in any team Markov game under its convergence conditions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses novelty detection by seeking a small region of input space containing a specified fraction of the underlying probability mass. Observations outside that region can then be treated as departures from the modeled data. The proposed single-class minimax probability machine frames this region-finding task through worst-case probabilistic reasoning.

Its distribution-free method uses only a distribution's mean and covariance matrix, without assuming a further distributional form. Given that information, it minimizes the worst-case probability that a point lies outside a convex set. This makes the available moment information central to the guarantee, while allowing the rest of the distribution's shape to remain unspecified.

The authors also develop a robust approach for estimating the mean and covariance in the general two-class MPM setting and explain how it specializes to the single-class case. This connects robust parameter estimation to the novelty-detection construction. Empirical comparisons include a single-class SVM and a two-class SVM method. The abstract states that these comparisons are provided, without asserting a particular winning method or performance margin.
neurips-2002-robust-novelty-detection-wi.tldr: Single-class MPM uses mean and covariance information to find a novelty-detection region through distribution-free worst-case probability reasoning.

paragraphs: The paper studies the relationship between what kernel principal components analysis observes in a finite sample and the corresponding structure of the underlying data distribution. On the sample side, the relevant object is a Gram matrix containing kernel evaluations between observations. On the distribution side, the authors consider a continuous eigenvalue problem.

Both objects have eigenvalues, collectively called their spectra. The authors bound the differences between the sample matrix's spectrum and the spectrum of the continuous problem associated with the sampling density. This directly connects quantities computed from the available observations to quantities defined by the underlying process from which those observations were drawn.

The analysis also provides a performance bound for kernel PCA. Its contribution is theoretical: it turns the relationship between finite-sample spectral information and the underlying continuous spectrum into quantitative bounds. That relationship matters because the method operates on sampled data while its interpretation concerns structure beyond those particular observations. The abstract establishes the existence of these bounds without specifying their formulas or numerical size.
neurips-2002-the-stability-of-kernel-pri.tldr: The paper bounds differences between sample and continuous kernel spectra and derives a performance bound for kernel PCA.

paragraphs: The paper asks how people can draw sophisticated causal conclusions from only one or a few observations. Its proposed explanation is that people bring substantial prior knowledge to the task. Intuitive theories shape which causal accounts they consider, helping explain how limited evidence can support judgments that would be difficult to derive from observations alone.

The authors formalize this idea as Bayesian reasoning over causal graphical models. Different graphs represent possible causal explanations, while prior knowledge shapes the space of hypotheses. Evidence is interpreted within that structured space, making the interaction between observations and existing beliefs central to the account of causal judgment.

Two case studies develop the approach, including quantitative models of human judgments and brief comparisons with traditional bottom-up inference models. These cases illustrate how theory-guided probabilistic reasoning can be used to explain human causal inference. The paper argues for this explanation rather than establishing that every causal judgment follows the same mechanism. Its main contribution is an explicit connection between intuitive theories, structured causal hypotheses, and learning from very little data.
neurips-2002-theory-based-causal-inferen.tldr: The paper models human causal judgments as Bayesian inference over causal graphs shaped by prior intuitive theories.

paragraphs: The paper develops a classification framework that uses both labeled and unlabeled examples. Its central assumption is that the data lie on a submanifold within a high-dimensional space. Under that assumption, the classifier is naturally defined on the lower-dimensional structure occupied by the data, making that structure the domain of the learning problem.

The Laplace–Beltrami operator supplies a basis for square-integrable functions on the manifold. Unlabeled examples are sufficient to recover such a basis, after which labeled examples train the classifier. This gives the two kinds of data distinct roles: unlabeled observations reveal the geometry used to represent functions, while labels determine the classification behavior within that representation.

For computation, the method represents the manifold using an adjacency graph of the data and approximates the continuous operator with a graph Laplacian. The paper considers applications to image and text classification. Its contribution is a principled connection between the manifold assumption and a practical learning procedure, showing how unlabeled observations can contribute a function space in which supervised training takes place.
neurips-2002-using-manifold-stucture-for.tldr: Assuming data lie on a manifold, the method uses unlabeled examples to construct a graph-based function basis and labeled examples to train a classifier.
